# Introduction {#sec-intro}

The previous study -- [Portfolio Optimization](https://konilo.github.io/sandbox/sandbox/portfolio_optimization/portfolio_optimization.html) -- set out to design a portfolio optimized for utility maximization which requires solving @eq-challenge.

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\text{return}}{\text{risk}}}_{\text{to maximize}} \times \underbrace{\text{leverage}}_{\substack{\text{to adapt to my} \\ \text{risk aversion level}}}
$$ {#eq-challenge}

The tool used to borrow cash and lever up the portfolio is a specific combination of options called a short box spread. This is the topic of this study.

Some key facts about short box spreads:

- they act as fixed-rate loans: get $x$ today and pay back $y$ on a given date, with $x$, $y$, and the term date being known from the start and fixed, and $x < y$;
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_spread
    https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/boxspread.asp
    https://earlyretirementnow.com/2021/12/09/low-cost-leverage-box-spread/
- they are accessible to French citizens (via a compte-titres ordinaire from the most sophisticated brokers such as Interactive Brokers);
    https://www.reddit.com/r/vosfinances/comments/1tqzjd4/cayas_meilleur_que_le_100_world/
    https://cayas.fr/le-journal/ouvrir-et-configurer-son-compte-interactive-brokers
- they surpass other forms of borrowing (such as consumer credit, lombard credit, leveraged ETFs) in terms of allocation constraints and rate, at the cost of additional complexity;
    https://youtu.be/fYO19-YkulI
- they require some expertise^[margin, options] and automated monitoring^[margin maintenance], which means that they are not suitable for all investors.


# Semantics

Find some fundamentals about options in Elton et al. ([2014](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/modern-portfolio-theory-and-investment-analysis-9th-edition-p-9781118469941); chapter 23), for instance. The main terms used herein are defined in @tbl-semantics.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Being long on an option | Having bought an option and holding it |
| Being short on an option | Having sold an option (which is not yet expired or exercised), aka having written an option |
| To long a call (LC) | Buying and holding a call |
| To long a put (LP) | Buying and holding a put |
| To short a call (SC) | Writing a call (which is not yet expired or exercised) |
| To short a put (SP) | Writing a put (which is not yet expired or exercised) |
| A box spread | (LC + SP) + (SC + LP), each parens being a leg |
| Leg 1 of a box spread | LC + SP at the same strike i.e., a synthetic long forward (Gantin, [2026](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/synthetic-forward-contract.asp)) |
| Leg 2 of a box spread | SC + LP at the same strike i.e., a synthetic short forward (ibid.) |
| To short a box spread | Having sold a box spread, i.e., borrowing cash^[A broker may present this trade as *buying* the reversed combination of options at a negative price: shorting a combination (to short (LC + SP) + (SC + LP)) is synonmous to buying its reverse (to long (SC + LP) + (LC + SP)).] |
| To long box spread | Having bought a box spread i.e., lending cash |
: Semantics {#tbl-semantics}


# Understanding a short box spread
## Variables

The variables used in this deconstruction of short box spreads are defined as follows:

- $K_1$ = the strike price of the 1st leg's options
- $K_2$ = the strike price of the 2nd leg's options
- $C_1$ = the premium of leg 1's call
- $C_2$ = the premium of leg 2's call
- $P_1$ = the premium of leg 1's put
- $P_2$ = the premium of leg 2's put
- $S_E$ = the price of the underlying security at expiration

Options control multiple shares of the underlying security (e.g., 100 or 10; we'll count this under the $m$ variable) but the literature's standard doesn't include a factor to account for this ^[from my experience, at least]. For accuracy, the formulas herein consider options controlling a single share. This choice only affects the option premiums which are divided by $m$ relative to the real ones.

Box spreads must be implemented using [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_style), [cash-settled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_(finance)#According_to_the_delivery_type) options. This study only considers options of this type.


## The payoff of each leg of a short box spread

| Part of the leg to short | Corresponding action | Now | At expiration | Ditto |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  | If $S_E > K_1$ | If $S_E \leq K_1$ |
| LC | Shorting a LC i.e., writing a call | $C_1$^[being paid the call's premium] | $(K_1 - S_E)$^[paying the call's intrinsic value $S_E - K_1$ in cash (as it is in the money)] | $0$^[the call expires worthless] |
| SP | Shorting a SP i.e., buying a put | $-P_1$^[paying the put's premium] | $0$^[the put expires worthless] | $(K_1 - S_E)$^[being paid the put's intrinsic value $K_1 - S_E$ in cash (as it is in the money)] |
| Total |  | $C_1-P_1$ | $(K_1 - S_E)$^[same payoff in both cases: it's a synthetic short forward (which allows one to sell the underlying security for a fixed price on a given, future date)] | $(K_1 - S_E)$ |
: Shorting leg 1 of the box spread {#tbl-leg1}

| Part of the leg to short | Corresponding action | Now | At expiration | Ditto |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|  |  |  | If $S_E > K_2$ | If $S_E \leq K_2$ |
| SC | Shorting a SC i.e., buying a call | $-C_2$^[paying the call's premium] | $(S_E - K_2)$^[being paid the call's intrinsic value $S_E - K_2$ in cash (as it is in the money)] | $0$^[the call expires worthless] |
| LP | Shorting a LP i.e., writing a put | $P_2$^[being paid the put's premium] | $0$^[the put expires worthless] | $(S_E - K_2)$^[paying the put's intrinsic value $K_2 - S_E$ in cash (as it is in the money)] |
| Total |  | $-C_2+P_2$ | $(S_E - K_2)$^[same payoff in both cases, it's a synthetic long forward (which allows one to buy the underlying security for a fixed price on a given, future date)] | $(S_E - K_2)$ |
: Shorting leg 2 of the box spread {#tbl-leg2}

While initiating a short box spread clearly consists in buying or selling calls and puts, the process to repay the resulting loan can be less intuitive and, I think, deserves some more explanations. A short box spread loan is generally repaid by letting its options be exercised or expire worthless on the expiration date. Settlement is made automatically in cash drawing from the CTO's cash^[or on margin if the cash balance is too low, which should be prevented by rolling the options earlier; more on that further down]. (Early repayment is also possible by going long on the same 4 options which cancels out the 8 options. It implies some rate risk, bid/ask spread costs, and trading fees.)

## Solving the cashflows

| Leg                   | Now                     | At expiration |
| --------------------- | ----------------------- | ------------- |
| 1: shorting (LC + SP) | $C_1-P_1$               | $(K_1 - S_E)$ |
| 2: shorting (SC + LP) | $-C_2+P_2 = -(C_2-P_2)$ | $(S_E - K_2)$ |
| Total                 | $C_1-P_1-(C_2-P_2)$     | $(K_1 - K_2)$ |
: Cashflows {#tbl-together}

The cashflow at expiration is now solved: $K_1 - K_2$, whatever $S_E$. But the cashflow "Now" is not, yet.

Longing a box spread pays a fixed amount on a given date: economically, the payoff is identical to the one of a [zero-coupon bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-coupon_bond). Hence, a short box spread behaves like a zero-coupon bond issued by a borrower: it provides some cash "Now" and costs another, larger amount ($K_2 - K_1$) at expiration. It ensues that the price "Now" is the present value of that future repayment: $$C_1-P_1-(C_2-P_2) = \frac{K_2-K_1}{(1+R)^T}$$ where

- $T$ = the time to expiration of the options, in years
- $R$ = the box spread's implied annual rate

No option pricing model is needed to solve this. The underlying's price $S_0$, its volatility, and its dividends all cancel out because both legs share the same underlying and expiration date. Only the implied rate -- the discount rate -- remains unknown.

The market sets the price of the box (i.e., the four premiums), and $R$ is the rate implied by that price. $R$ is not predictable beforehand, but is fixed as soon as the orders are filled. The premiums land between the alternatives of both sides:

- lenders (longing the box spread) require $R$ above what they would otherwise earn on the currency in question e.g., the yield of German government bills/notes (Bubill/Schatz) or of US Treasury bills/notes of the same term;
- borrowers (shorting the box spread) require $R$ below what they would otherwise pay on the same currency e.g., their broker's [margin rate](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/trading/margin-rates.php) for EUR or USD.

Empirically, $R$ lands slightly above the risk-free rate of the currency and term in question^[The following figures are ballpark indications: the implied rate of a given box can be computed from its quotes in one's own brokerage account before committing (see further down).]:

- USD (options on the SPX index): the Treasury bill yield + 0.2 to 0.3 percentage points (pp) (ERN, [2021](https://earlyretirementnow.com/2021/12/09/low-cost-leverage-box-spread/));
- EUR (options on the ESTX50 index): about 3.0 to 3.3% for 1-year boxes in November 2026 ([Yieldbard](https://yieldbard.com/), 2026); forum users report fills at IBKR's EUR reference rate curve + about 0.1 to 0.2 pp (Cayas forum, [2026](https://forum.cayas.fr/t/box-spread-pour-financer-sa-vie-vs-credit-lombard-le-hack-sous-cote-ou-usine-a-gaz/1462/37)); and Cayas assumes Euribor 3 months + 0.1 to 0.5 pp in its backtests ([2026](https://cayas.fr/le-journal/msci-world-assurance-vie-pilotee-allocation-cayas-meilleure)).

For comparison:
- a broker's margin loan costs IBKR's reference benchmark rate^[A rate IBKR computes for each currency from "internationally recognized reference rates [...], bank deposit rates, and dynamic interbank rates" ([IBKR](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/trading/margin-benchmarks.php)); 2.485% for EUR on 12 Nov 2026.] + 1.5 pp up to €90k and + 1 point up to €900k, i.e., 3.99% and 3.49% in EUR on 15 Nov 2026 ([IBKR](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/trading/margin-rates.php));
- and a lombard credit €STR + 0.7 to 1.95 pp (Cayas forum, [2026](https://forum.cayas.fr/t/box-spread-pour-financer-sa-vie-vs-credit-lombard-le-hack-sous-cote-ou-usine-a-gaz/1462)).

## Putting it together

Scaling back to real index options: their premiums and strikes are quoted in index points, and each contract pays a fixed currency amount per index point, its multiplier $m$ (100 USD for SPX options, 10 EUR for ESTX50 options, as per their contract's description provided by one's broker). For instance, an ESTX50 box spread with strikes 4150 and 8650 repays $10 \times (8650 - 4150) =$ €45,000 at expiration. Assuming the legs are built such that $K_1 < K_2$, shorting a box spread:

- initially provides $$\frac{m(K_2-K_1)}{(1+R)^T}$$; that's the present value of the difference between the two strikes, using the borrowing rate;
- and costs $$m(K_1 - K_2)$$ at expiration; that's the (negative) difference between the two strikes.

Receive a given amount today, and pay back more, eventually.

## Computing the rate

Rearranging the equation for the cashflow "Now" gives the implied interest rate: $$R = \left(\frac{K_2-K_1}{C_1-P_1-(C_2-P_2)}\right)^{1/T} - 1$$ with all terms in index points.

The four options are traded together, as a single order with a single limit price for the whole box. Plugging a candidate limit price into this formula gives the corresponding rate, so the rate is known before submitting the order. Comparing it with references tells whether the limit price is sensible: a rate well above them means accepting to borrow more expensively than necessary; a rate well below them means the order is unlikely to be executed, as lenders can earn more elsewhere. References:

- [boxtrades.com](https://www.boxtrades.com/) publishes the SPX box spread yield curve, derived from trades;
- [Yieldbard](https://yieldbard.com/) publishes ESTX50 and SPX box spread yield curves and recent trades (the EUR curve is not derived from trades but from closing prices);
- IBKR's TWS shows its reference EUR and USD rate curves^[New Window > Option Analysis > Interactive Analytics > Interest Rate; used as such by forum members ([Cayas forum, 2026](https://forum.cayas.fr/t/box-spread-pour-financer-sa-vie-vs-credit-lombard-le-hack-sous-cote-ou-usine-a-gaz/1462/37))].
- the [Box tab of Portfolio Construction](https://portfolio-construction.freeboxos.fr/?section=box.interest-rate-swap-curves#box) takes a target rate and returns the corresponding limit price.


# Sizing a short box spread loan

- The amount owed at expiration date (= the **face** of the loan) is $$face = m \times N_{boxes} \times -(K_1 - K_2)$$ ^[The added "$-$" just converts the negative cashflow expression from above into a positive amount]. It's controlled by both
	- the strike width $K_1-K_2$ of the boxe(s)
	- and the number of boxes sold $N_{boxes}$

```{r}
#| label: fig-payoff
#| fig-cap: "Cashflows at expiration of a short ESTX50 box spread with $K_1 = 4150$ and $K_2 = 8650$, in index points per box (× 10 EUR). Whatever $S_E$, the box costs $K_2 - K_1 = 4500$ points (€45,000) at expiration; the cash received now, $4500 / 1.03$ ≈ 4369 points (≈ €43,689), assumes a 1-year term at a 3% rate."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 10

K1 <- 4150
K2 <- 8650
R  <- 0.03 # illustrative 1-year rate, for the cash received now
S  <- seq(3000, 10000, by = 10)

colors <- c("Leg 1" = "#2a78d6", "Leg 2" = "#eb6834", "Box" = "#3d3d3a")
options_order <- c("Leg 1: short call K1", "Leg 1: long put K1", "Leg 2: long call K2", "Leg 2: short put K2")

options_dt <- rbindlist(list(
    data.table(group = "Leg 1", line = options_order[1], S = S, y = -pmax(S - K1, 0)),
    data.table(group = "Leg 1", line = options_order[2], S = S, y =  pmax(K1 - S, 0)),
    data.table(group = "Leg 2", line = options_order[3], S = S, y =  pmax(S - K2, 0)),
    data.table(group = "Leg 2", line = options_order[4], S = S, y = -pmax(K2 - S, 0))
))
options_dt[, line := factor(line, levels = options_order)]
legs_dt <- rbindlist(list(
    data.table(group = "Leg 1", line = "leg 1: K1 - S_E", S = S, y = K1 - S),
    data.table(group = "Leg 2", line = "leg 2: S_E - K2", S = S, y = S - K2)
))
box_dt <- rbindlist(list(
    data.table(group = "Box", line = sprintf("repaid at expiration: K1 - K2 = %s points (€%s)", format(K1 - K2, big.mark = ","), format(10 * (K2 - K1), big.mark = ",")), type = "solid", S = S, y = K1 - K2),
    data.table(group = "Box", line = sprintf("received now: (K2 - K1) / (1 + R) ≈ %s points (≈ €%s)", format(round((K2 - K1) / (1 + R)), big.mark = ","), format(round(10 * (K2 - K1) / (1 + R)), big.mark = ",")), type = "dashed", S = S, y = (K2 - K1) / (1 + R))
))

y_limits <- range(c(options_dt$y, legs_dt$y, box_dt$y))
base_layers <- list(
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4),
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(K1, K2), color = "grey70", linetype = "dotted"),
    scale_color_manual(values = colors, guide = "none"),
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(K1, K2), labels = c("K1", "K2")),
    scale_y_continuous(limits = y_limits, expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)),
    labs(x = expression(S[E]), y = "points"),
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10),
    theme(
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
    )
)

p_options <- ggplot(options_dt, aes(S, y, color = group)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~line, ncol = 2) +
    ggtitle("1. The four options") +
    base_layers

p_legs <- ggplot(legs_dt, aes(S, y, color = group)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_text(
        data = legs_dt[, .SD[which.max(S)], by = line],
        aes(label = line, vjust = fifelse(y < 0, 1.6, -0.6)),
        hjust = 1, size = 3, color = "grey20"
    ) +
    ggtitle("2. The two legs (sums of their options)") +
    base_layers

p_box <- ggplot(box_dt, aes(S, y, color = group)) +
    geom_line(aes(linetype = type), linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_text(
        data = box_dt[, .SD[which.min(abs(S - (K1 + K2) / 2))], by = line],
        aes(label = line), vjust = 1.6, size = 3, color = "grey20"
    ) +
    scale_linetype_identity() +
    ggtitle("3. The box (sum of the legs)") +
    base_layers

p_options / p_legs / p_box + plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1, 1))
```
